newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Rebels advance on Kabul, defenders vow to fight on.
newsitem.headline: Rebels advance on Kabul, defenders vow to fight on.

text.p: Afghanistan's rebel Taleban Islamic militia advanced on the Afghan capital Kabul on Thursday as the defending government forces threw up new defences and vowed to fight to death.

"We are establishing defences in every street of Kabul," a spokesman for the beleaguered government told reporters as the two sides fought on in the city's outskirts, ignoring a U.N. Security Council call for an immediate ceasefire.

Taleban sources in neighbouring Pakistan said the militia forces, which control most of Afghanistan and seek to oust President Burhanuddin Rabbani to enforce a strict Islamic order in the country, had penetrated the city from the east and were only five km (three miles) from the presidential palace.

Official sources denied this but government fighters guarding the main road east of Kabul said the rebels had seized the nearby military academy hours after a spokesman said it was in government hands.
Government troops feverishly dug new positions in the prestigious Mickroryan housing district in eastern Kabul early in the evening while tanks also made defensive manoeuvres.
But Taleban sources in Pakistan later said the militia had entered Mickroray area and were battling government forces there. There was no independent confirmation of this report.
Witnesses in Kabul said fighting in the east appeared to have intensified as darkness fell with rockets landing in the city. But there was no word on casualties.
Government fighters said the Taleban were trying to advance on a new road to the government's main airbase at Bagram, north of Kabul. The old road to Bagram was in government hands.
A tank in the middle of the road fired at Taleban positions while small arms fire could also be heard in the north.
"We have thousands of volunteers from the city," said Amrullah, spokesman for Rabbani's top military commander Ahmad Shah Masood.
"We are not short of ammunition, fuel, morale or motive. We will remain in Kabul whether we are on the earth or beneath it."
Amrullah said the Taleban had lost hundreds of men to reach the eastern outskirts of Pul-i-Charkhi "and will perhaps lose thousands in Kabul".
Several people in Mickroryan area were leaving with goods on handcarts.
"We are leaving because of Taleban rocketing in our area," said Zehrullah, 35, who said he has been a fighter for Masood.

An official of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), Jan-Luc Paladini, said there had been hundreds of dead and wounded on both sides in the past two days of fighting, but he had no details.
He said the ICRC had medical stocks in Kabul to last for six months and the ICRC relief department had been bringing more over the past few days.

The ICRC on Thursday stopped all flights from Bagram to the Pakistani city of Peshawar, fearing the military situation could worsen, after evacuating 50 people, including 16 ICRC delegates, leaving only staff needed for emergencies.
But Paladini said: "The ICRC is staying in Kabul. We are not leaving."

Earlier, Kabul city itself was calm, and shops and markets were open with no visible sign of panic. But hundreds of people were leaving the city on the road north towards Mazar-i-Sharif in trucks and buses packed with belongings on roofs.
"The Taleban are coming, one hundred percent," an Afghan aid worker said.

"They (government fighters) set up a machine-gun in my street so I thought I had better leave," said Jeff Arnold, programme officer of the German Agro-Action relief agency. "I hope this will all be over quickly so we can come back."
Taleban sources in Pakistan said the militia had further advanced from the south into the shattered city, taken Pul-i-Charkhi and the nearby military academy and Bagrami district in the southeast.

Calling the defence of Kabul "a war of identity", Amrullah accused Pakistan of sending military technicians to help the Taleban and said other countries, which he refused to name, were also aiding the rebels.
"We are defending the country's pride against Pakistani puppets. Pakistan wants to control our country. We are ready to give as much sacrifice as required. We don't mind if we die."
But Pakistan denied the accusations.
"We have had and will continue to observe total neutrality while we must maintain a close watch on the events as they develop," a Pakistan Foreign Ministry spokesman said in Islamabad.
The 15-nation U.N. Security Council appealed for a ceasefire and peace talks after a meeting in New York on Wednesday.
Amrullah criticised the United Nations for what he said was inaction when Kabul was on the verge of a catastrophe.
"They know there could be a massacre in Kabul and massive violation of so-called human rights, but they are just watching," he said.
"Kabul is everything. It's the capital. It's the symbol of Afghan identity and we will defend it."
